props.title: A Short Film About Killing

sections.content: A Short Film About Killing (1988) represents Polish director Krzysztof Kieślowski's most brutal and unflinching examination of state violence. Expanded from Episode 5 of his Dekalog (1989) series, this devastating portrait follows two acts of murder - one by a troubled young man, the other by the state through capital punishment. Kieślowski uses sickly green filters and vignetted frames to create a suffocating atmosphere that makes Warsaw feel like a concrete prison. The murder scene remains one of cinema's most disturbing sequences, deliberately prolonged to emphasize the messy, unglamorous reality of taking a life.

sections.content: The film sparked crucial debates about capital punishment in Poland, contributing to its eventual abolition. Its influence can be traced through later anti-death penalty films like Dead Man Walking (1995) and Monster (2003), though few match its raw power. Kieślowski's technique of showing both murder and execution as equally barbaric acts was revolutionary, forcing viewers to confront their own complicity in state-sanctioned killing.

The film's visual style influenced a generation of European directors. The grimy urban alienation echoes through works like La Haine (1995) and Lilya 4-Ever (2002). Kieślowski's use of color filters and claustrophobic framing became a blueprint for depicting moral decay in Eastern European cinema, seen in films like 4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days (2007). sections.content: Contemporary filmmakers continue drawing from Kieślowski's unflinching moral examination. The White Ribbon (2009) and Son of Saul (2015) share his ability to depict violence without sensationalism. His influence extends beyond Europe - Monster (2003) and In Cold Blood (1967) similarly examine the psychology of killing while questioning society's right to execute criminals.
